cards.text: Just before this, she told the daughters of Jerusalem that her beloved had gone down to his garden (Song of Solomon 6:2), and she said she belongs to her beloved and he belongs to her (Song of Solomon 6:3). Now he's the one talking, and he calls her "my darling." Friend, this man showed up with a LIST, and he is not reading it quietly.

cards.question: He tells his darling she's as beautiful as Tirzah, a city in Israel (1 Kings 15:33). Which other city does he say she's as lovely as?

cards.text: Then he says she's as majestic as troops with banners. Not a flower, friend, an ARMY with its flags flying.

cards.question: Next he asks his darling to turn her eyes away from him, because they have ___ him.
He says his darling's hair is like a flock of goats streaming down from Gilead. What picture is he painting of her hair?

cards.text: Now her teeth, like a flock of sheep coming up from the washing. Nobody's ever praised MY teeth, friend, because all I've got is a mustache and a dream.

cards.question: When he says each of his darling's teeth has its twin and not one is lost, he's picturing a full matched set with nothing missing.

cards.text: Then her brow behind her veil is like a slice of pomegranate. Goats, sheep and now a fruit: this man is painting her a whole countryside, and he is NOT slowing down.
Now he brings up a crowd: sixty queens, eighty concubines and maidens without number.

cards.question: But next to all those queens, concubines and maidens, his dove, his perfect one, is ___.
The man in the song says his dove is the favorite of the mother who bore her.

cards.text: Now the maidens, the queens and the concubines all get a look at his dove. That's a LOT of eyes, friend, and I'd be sweating flour.

cards.question: When the maidens see his dove, what do they do?

answers.text: They ask where she came from

cards.question: Like the maidens, the queens and concubines praise the man's dove when they see her.

cards.text: Then a question rings out about her, and the text leaves open who's asking. I bet whoever it is just stood there with their mouth hanging open.

cards.question: A question rings out about the man's dove, asking who this is who shines. What does the question picture her shining like?

cards.text: The dawn, the moon, the sun and the stars in procession. My Berry would've had his face pressed to the kitchen window ALL night for this one.
Then a voice speaks, and the text doesn't say whose. It says, "I went down to the walnut grove to see the blossoms of the valley".

cards.question: At the walnut grove, the speaker went to see if the vines were ___ or the pomegranates were in bloom.

cards.text: Then the speaker says desire set them among the royal chariots of their people. One minute it's blossoms, the next minute it's CHARIOTS.

cards.question: The speaker who went down to the walnut grove knew all along that their desire would set them among the royal chariots.

cards.text: The speaker says it happened before they realized it. That's me with the oven timer, friend: I check ONE batch, and next thing I know I've boxed three hundred cookies.

findings.problem: The opening card never says who "she" is. It starts with "she told the daughters of Jerusalem" and "her beloved" without saying simply who either of them is, so the baker doesn't know who is being spoken to.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on. If the passage starts in the middle of a thought, it gives the context.

findings.problem: The woman and the daughters of Jerusalem show up here for the first time, but neither is introduced.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: This blank only asks the baker to guess the wording of a line. No earlier card sets up why the speaker wants her eyes turned away, so "judged" is as reasonable a pick as "overcome." A right answer comes down to luck, not reasoning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "They ask where she came from" is close to the question in 6:10 ("Who is this who shines like the dawn..."). The text leaves open who asks that question, and it could be the maidens and queens of 6:9. A baker could argue this answer is right.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: This card adds nothing new. Card 12 already told 6:12, and card 13 already asked and answered "before I realized it." The card's first sentence just repeats that answer, so it doesn't move the passage forward. The joke could ride on card 12 instead.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: The BSB text given has no speaker headings, and 6:4-10 never says who the speaker is. Even so, stop 1 card 1 says "Now he's the one talking," and later cards call the speaker "he" and "the man in the song." Stop 2 cards 10, 12 and 13 do the opposite: they leave the speaker of 6:11-12 open. Card 10 also quotes an "I" line without naming who says it.
findings.question: In the Song of Solomon, can Papa Dorin name the speaker (the man, the woman, the friends) the way the BSB section headings do, even though the verse text doesn't? The opening card has to say who is speaking, and "Who's speaking" says to name an "I" speaker first. But "Leave open what the text leaves open" covers who is speaking. If he can't name the speaker, what should the opening card and the "I" quotes say instead?
